sourceIssues.locator: §4.3, proof of Lemma 4.3.15, case of an integral domain, p. 722, citing Lemma 4.2.16 and Remark 4.2.17 (p. 710); the same passage appears in arXiv v1
sourceIssues.printed: For this, assume first that R is an integral domain, with quotient field K. By Lemma 4.2.16 (cf. Remark 4.2.17), the functor from p-divisible groups over R to p-divisible groups over K is fully faithful. We can find an isogeny ψ′_K : G_K → G_{0,K} of degree bounded only in terms of h, which then extends to a map ψ′ : G → G_{0,R} of degree bounded only in terms of h.
sourceIssues.correction: Let K̄ be an algebraic closure of K and R̄ the integral closure of R in K̄. R̄ is an integral domain that is integral over the strictly henselian ring R, so it is local and strictly henselian. It is integrally closed and perfect, and its residue field is k, because k is perfect and separably closed and hence algebraically closed. Over K̄, the Dieudonné–Manin classification gives an isogeny ψ′_{K̄} : G_{K̄} → G_{0,K̄} of degree bounded in terms of h. Apply Lemma 4.2.16 on each valuation ring of K̄ containing R̄; the intersection of these rings is R̄. Hence both ψ′_{K̄} and p^N(ψ′_{K̄})^{−1} extend over R̄, so ψ′_{K̄} extends to an isogeny ψ′ : G_{R̄} → G_{0,R̄} of bounded degree. Correcting at k as printed gives a quasi-isogeny ψ_{R̄} : G_{R̄} → G_{0,R̄} that lifts ψ_k and for which p^cψ_{R̄} and p^cψ_{R̄}^{−1} are isogenies. The ring B = R̄ ⊗_R R̄ is perfect and integral over R, and it has a single prime over the closed point, with residue field k. So B is a strictly henselian perfect local ring. The two pullbacks of ψ_{R̄} to B both lift ψ_k, so they agree by the uniqueness of lifts proved at the start of the proof: after inverting p, homomorphisms between constant groups over a connected perfect ring inject into homomorphisms over k. Since R → R̄ is injective and integral, Spec R̄ → Spec R is a v-cover, and [BS17, Th. 4.1(i)] gives R = {f ∈ R̄ : f ⊗ 1 = 1 ⊗ f in B}. Choose R-bases of the Hopf algebras of the p^n-torsion. The matrices of p^cψ_{R̄} and p^cψ_{R̄}^{−1} in these bases then have entries in R, so ψ_{R̄} descends to the required quasi-isogeny ψ : G → G_{0,R}. The case of several minimal primes then applies this to each R/𝔭_i, as printed.
sourceIssues.reason:
Two steps of the domain case are unsupported. The statements they are used for are true, so this is a gap and not an error.

(1) Full faithfulness from R to K is taken from Lemma 4.2.16 via Remark 4.2.17. Checking matrix entries on the valuation rings of K that contain R only shows that the entries lie in the integral closure of R. So the argument covers only integrally closed domains. In fact Remark 4.2.17 is false as stated for non-normal domains. Take p odd and the perfection of the nodal cubic y² = x²(x+1). There, the étale group Q_p/Z_p twisted by the sign character of the loop has no nonzero homomorphism to Q_p/Z_p, but it becomes constant over the fraction field.

Strictly henselian perfect domains need not be integrally closed. For a prime ℓ ≠ p, take the perfection of the strict henselisation at the origin of F̄_p[x^ℓ] + yF̄_p[x, y]. This is a strictly henselian perfect domain, and it contains x^ℓ. The element x = xy/y lies in its fraction field and is a root of T^ℓ − x^ℓ, but x is not in the ring, because no x^{p^n} is. The same applies to the rings R/𝔭_i of the general case. For strictly henselian perfect domains the asserted full faithfulness does hold, but only as a consequence of the lemma being proved.

(2) The isogeny ψ′_K is asserted to exist over K, but K is only perfect, not algebraically closed. For example, if R is the perfection of F̄_p[[t]], then x^p − x = t^{−1} has no root in K. Over such a field the Dieudonné–Manin classification does not apply: an étale group whose Tate module carries a nontrivial character of Gal(K̄/K) is not isogenous over K to any group defined over F̄_p. That G_K is isogenous to a constant group depends on G extending over the strictly henselian ring R, and the argument never uses this.

Both steps are repaired by working over the integral closure of R in K̄ and then descending. The descent uses only two things the paper already has: the uniqueness of lifts (called "necessarily unique" on p. 722 and proved in the first paragraph of the proof) and the v-descent [BS17, Th. 4.1(i)] used on p. 723. So Lemma 4.3.15 and Remark 4.3.16 stand, and only their proof is affected. They serve Proposition 4.3.13 (Proposition 1.13 in the introduction), which the paper says is not used later (p. 720).
sourceIssues.known: No erratum or later correction of this step is known. The passage is unchanged from arXiv v1 to the published version. Footnote 22 (p. 722) cites [OZ02, Cor. 3.6] for the special case where R is the perfection of a noetherian strictly henselian ring and G is defined over that ring.

sourceIssues.locator: §4.4 (Étale cohomology), opening paragraph, p. 726; the same sentence is in arXiv v1, §4.4
sourceIssues.printed: In this section, we make the additional assumption that 𝒮_{K_pK^p} is proper over 𝒪_{E,𝔭}. It is known that this is equivalent to asking that G is anisotropic over ℚ; cf. [Lan11].
sourceIssues.correction: … It is known that this is equivalent to asking that G^ad is anisotropic over ℚ, i.e. that G is anisotropic modulo its centre (equivalently, G has no proper parabolic ℚ-subgroup, or the Shimura varieties Sh_K are compact); cf. [Lan11].
sourceIssues.reason: Here G is the PEL group of §4.3 (p. 713), G(R) = {x ∈ End_{B⊗R}(V⊗R) : xx* ∈ R^×}. For t ∈ R^×, the scalar t·id_V is B-linear and has adjoint t, so its similitude factor is t². Hence t ↦ t·id_V embeds 𝔾_m into the centre of G, and G always contains a nontrivial central ℚ-split torus. Read literally, "G is anisotropic over ℚ" therefore never holds, yet the compact PEL Shimura varieties of §6.3 (p. 756) are proper. The intended condition is anisotropy modulo the centre, i.e. G^ad is ℚ-anisotropic. For a connected reductive group this is equivalent to having no proper parabolic ℚ-subgroup. By Borel–Harish-Chandra and Mostow–Tamagawa it is equivalent to compactness of the Shimura varieties, and [Lan11] passes from a proper generic fibre to a proper integral model 𝒮_{K_pK^p} over 𝒪_{E,𝔭}. The page image shows the same loose usage on p. 651 ("an anisotropic unitary similitude group"), so the intended meaning is clear. The working hypothesis of §4.4, and hence of Theorem 4.4.4 (p. 729), is properness of 𝒮_{K_pK^p} itself. The reformulation is used only when §6.3 applies §4.4 to a compact Shimura variety, and it holds in the corrected form. No stated result or proof changes.

sourceIssues.reason: On the page image of p. 727, the first display of the proof reads "Spa(C(x), C(x)^+) ∼ lim_{←j} Spa(R_j, R_j^+)". Both arguments have a plain x with no bar. A magnified image shows this clearly, and the bar on x̄ is clearly printed in "neighborhoods of x̄" in the line just above and in "(R^i f_*G)_x̄" just below, so this is not a text-layer artefact. The statement of Lemma 4.4.1 on p. 726 introduces only C(x̄): a completed algebraic closure of the residue field K(x), with an open and bounded valuation subring C(x̄)^+ lifting K(x)^+. It gives the geometric point x̄ = Spa(C(x̄), C(x̄)^+) → X and the fibre Y_x̄ = (Y ×_X Spa(C(x̄), C(x̄)^+))^∧. No field C(x) is defined in this context. The only other use of the symbol, on p. 684 in §3, belongs to an unrelated argument about points of Spa(R, R^+). The proof takes the limit over a cofinal system U_j = Spa(R_j, R_j^+) of affinoid étale neighbourhoods of x̄. That limit is the geometric point x̄ = Spa(C(x̄), C(x̄)^+), and this is what the next step needs: Y_x̄ ∼ lim_j Y ×_X Spa(R_j, R_j^+). So the display must be read with C(x̄) and C(x̄)^+. With it, the correct identity is tr π_p(φ^n⃗_p) = tr(Red^b_n⃗(π_p))(φ_p·δ̄^{1/2}_{P(ν_b)}). The twist is not harmless when b is non-basic. Then s·ν_b is a non-central cocharacter, (sν_b)(p) is central in both M_b and J_b, and δ̄_{P(ν_b)}((sν_b)(p)) is a nontrivial power of p. Comparing absolute values of central characters at this element shows that ρ ⊗ δ̄^{1/2} ≠ ρ for every nonzero virtual representation ρ of J_b(ℚ_p). Twisting by high powers of Frobenius, as in [Shi11, Lemma 6.4], shows the difference is detected by an acceptable φ_p. So Lemma 5.4.2 as printed fails whenever the untwisted composite is nonzero. An example is b µ-ordinary, n⃗ = (n) and π_p an unramified principal series, where J_b = M_b, LJ is the identity and the Jacquet module is nonzero. Lemma 5.5.1, the identity before Corollary 5.6.2 (obtained "making use of Lemma 5.4.2") and Corollary 5.6.2 are stated in terms of Red, so they are off by the same twist. The fix is a one-line change to the definition, and it is clearly what the authors intended, since the proof cites Shin's lemma for the twisted map. Twisting by a character preserves vanishing, so Lemma 5.4.3, Theorem 5.5.7, Corollary 5.6.3 and the main theorems are unaffected.

sourceIssues.reason:
The paper builds the test function at ∞ from the endoscopic parameters, not from the trivial representation of G_n⃗. On p. 735, φ^n⃗_∞ is a combination of Euler–Poincaré functions over the parameters φ_{G_n⃗} with η̃∘φ_{G_n⃗} corresponding to the trivial representation of G_ℂ. On p. 737, f^n⃗_∞ is the matching combination of twisted Lefschetz functions f_{𝔾_n⃗,Ξ(φ_n⃗)} ([Shi11, (6.7)]). The twisted trace of Π^n⃗_∞ against f_{𝔾_n⃗,Ξ} vanishes unless Π^n⃗_∞ is Ξ-cohomological, so the argument of the proof shows that each contributing Π^n⃗_∞ is Ξ(φ_n⃗)-cohomological.

For n⃗ = (n_1, n_2) with n_1, n_2 > 0, no such Ξ(φ_n⃗) is trivial. By p. 745, ζ̃ multiplies the i-th block by ϖ^{e_i} with e_i = ε(n−n_i) ∈ {0, 1}; in [Shi11, (6.3)] the exponent is n−m_i ≥ 0 instead. By p. 746, ϖ_∞(z) = (z/z̄)^{δ/2} with δ odd. So if Ξ_i is trivial, the i-th block contributes a run of n_i consecutive exponents centred at e_iδ/2. The n exponents (n+1−2j)/2 of the trivial parameter split into two such runs only with centres n_2/2 and −n_1/2, or −n_2/2 and n_1/2. These have opposite signs, while e_1δ/2 and e_2δ/2 have the same sign or vanish. For example, take n = 3, n⃗ = (2, 1). Each of the three ways of distributing the exponents {1, 0, −1} between the blocks gives a nontrivial Ξ(φ_n⃗).

Read literally, the lemma would therefore force every term with n⃗ ≠ (n) to vanish. That is false in general. In [Shi11, Th. 6.1(ii)] (Case END, ξ may be trivial), the weights of Ξ_1 and Ξ_2 come from a partition of those of ξ, and the endoscopic term Red^b_{m_1,m_2}(π_{H,p}) survives. For a fixed Hecke eigensystem it is not a multiple of the stable term Red^b_n(π_p).

The later results are unaffected. The lemma is used on p. 744 (“Π^n⃗_∞ is cohomological, which implies Π^n⃗ is C-algebraic”, and the regularity of the infinitesimal character in the proof of Theorem 5.5.4), in Corollary 5.5.2, in Corollary 5.5.5, on p. 750 and in the proof of Theorem 5.5.7. All of these need only cohomology for some algebraic coefficient system, or only the form of the terms. The parenthesis “(recall that for us ξ is trivial)” on p. 744 is also correct: it concerns the twist in [Shi11, (6.2)], which is by a character of A_{G_n⃗,∞} and is trivial when ξ is trivial, whatever φ_n⃗ is. So only the stated clause of Lemma 5.5.1 is wrong; Theorems 5.5.4 and 5.5.7 stand.

The proof expresses the trace as a function of (f^n)^S ∈ ℋ^ur(𝔾_n(𝔸^S)) in two ways: once through the terms of Lemma 5.5.1, and once through the Π^S that occur in the cohomology. Remark 5.5.3 notes that several n⃗ can give the same Π^S, and the terms from different n⃗ carry signs that can cancel.

This cancellation happens within the paper's own setting. Take the setting of [Shi11], which satisfies the assumptions of §5.1, in Case END of [Shi11, §6.1]: m_1 > m_2, m_1 + m_2 = n, Π_H = ψ_H ⊗ Π_1 ⊗ Π_2, and Π = ζ̃_{m_1,m_2,*}(Π_H) = n-Ind(Π_M). The terms of Lemma 5.5.1 for n⃗ = (n) (the representation Π) and for n⃗ = (m_1, m_2) (the representation Π_H) have the same Hecke eigensystem. By [Shi11, Th. 6.1(ii), (6.6)], the Π^S-part of the Igusa cohomology is ½(e_1 Red^b_n(π_p) + e_2 Red^b_{m_1,m_2}(π_{H,p})), with e_i = ±1. By [Shi11, Lemma 5.9], Red^b_n(π_p) = e_p(J_b) π_{p,0} ⊗ (X_1 + X_2) ⊗ (⊗_{i>1} π_{w_i}) and Red^b_{m_1,m_2}(π_{H,p}) = e_p(J_b) π_{p,0} ⊗ (X_1 − X_2) ⊗ (⊗_{i>1} π_{w_i}). So only X_2 survives when e_1 = −e_2.

The case e_1 = −e_2 does occur. By [Shi11, Cor. 6.5(ii)], e_1 = (−1)^{n−1}. By [Shi11, Lemma 7.3], for m_2 = 1 exactly one of the two admissible characters χ, χ′ taken as Π_2 gives e_2 = e_1, so the other gives e_2 = −e_1.

Now take b with h(b) = m_2, and take π_{M,w,1} essentially square-integrable (for example, Π_1 supercuspidal at w). Since h < m_1, X_2 = 0. On the other hand, X_1 = LJ_{m_1}(π_{M,w,1}) ⊗ π_{M,w,2} ≠ 0. Then the term of Π in Lemma 5.5.1 is ±½ e_p(J_b) π_{p,0} ⊗ X_1 ⊗ (⊗_{i>1} π_{w_i}), which is nonzero, so Π contributes in the sense set up by the proof. But the Π^S-part of the cohomology is zero in the Grothendieck group, because BC is injective at the split places in S_fin. So Π^S does not occur, and the first assertion fails as printed.

Only the aggregate reading, in which the Hecke eigensystem as a whole contributes, is true, and that is what the proof establishes. Later arguments use only the converse direction or the aggregate form: Corollary 5.5.5, Theorem 5.5.7 (whose vanishing argument applies to every Π^{n⃗′} with the same Π), Corollary 5.6.3, and the proof of Theorem 6.3.1. sourceIssues.locator: §6.3, proof of Theorem 6.3.1, parts (1) and (2), p. 759 (also in arXiv v1)
sourceIssues.printed: Part (1): “By Poincaré duality (and applying the same discussion with the “dual” set of Hecke eigenvalues), the same holds true for compactly supported cohomology. We have a decomposition [H_c(𝓘^b_Mant, ℚ̄_ℓ)]^{S ur} = [H_c(𝓘^b_Mant, ℚ̄_ℓ)]^{S ur}_𝔪 + [H_c(𝓘^b_Mant, ℚ̄_ℓ)]^{S ur,𝔪} …”. Part (2): “As above, we take some b ∈ B(G, µ^{−1}) with d = ⟨2ρ, ν_b⟩ minimal such that H^i(Ig^b, 𝔽_ℓ)_𝔪 ≠ 0 for some i ∈ ℤ. We get concentration in middle degree in this case, and hence the argument above shows that there is some Galois representation r lifting ρ_𝔪 with BC^p([H_c(𝓘^b_Mant, ℚ̄_ℓ)]^{S ur})_r ≠ 0.”
sourceIssues.correction: Let 𝔪^∨ be the image of 𝔪 under the involution [K_qgK_q] ↦ [K_qg^{−1}K_q] of 𝕋^S. Since the 𝓘^b_{Mant,m} are smooth of dimension d, Poincaré duality turns the concentration of H^*(𝓘^b_{Mant,m}, ℤ_ℓ)_𝔪 in degree d (b minimal for 𝔪) into concentration of H_c^*(𝓘^b_{Mant,m}, ℤ_ℓ)_{𝔪^∨} in degree d, nonzero for m large; so Lemma 5.5.1 and Corollaries 5.5.2 and 5.5.5 give a lift r of ρ_{𝔪^∨} with BC^S([H_c(𝓘^b_Mant, ℚ̄_ℓ)]^{S ur})_r ≠ 0. ρ_{𝔪^∨} is a twist of the dual of ρ_𝔪 (Frobenius eigenvalues q_v^{n−1}α^{−1}), and the condition λ_a/λ_b ∉ {1, q} is unchanged under inversion and twisting, so ρ_{𝔪^∨} is decomposed generic at the same primes (the paper's remark that the dual ideal satisfies the same hypothesis). Hence in part (2) Lemma 6.2.2 and Theorem 5.5.7 applied to r show that the b minimal for 𝔪 is µ-ordinary, and the proof continues as printed. In part (1), choose b minimal for 𝔪^∨ instead (possible by Poincaré duality on S_K), or obtain ρ_𝔪 from ρ_{𝔪^∨} by dualizing and twisting, as in Caraiani–Scholze, Ann. of Math. 199 (2024), Corollary 5.1.3.
sourceIssues.reason: The cup-product pairing makes each Hecke operator adjoint to its transpose, so Poincaré duality identifies H_c^i(𝓘^b_{Mant,m})_𝔪 with the dual (up to twist) of H^{2d−i}(𝓘^b_{Mant,m})_{𝔪^∨}, not of H^{2d−i}(𝓘^b_{Mant,m})_𝔪. Corollary 6.1.4 applied to b minimal for 𝔪 therefore gives concentration of compactly supported cohomology only at 𝔪^∨; “the same discussion with the dual set” would give it at 𝔪 only for a b minimal for 𝔪^∨, and in general 𝔪^∨ ≠ 𝔪. In part (1) the choice of b does not matter, but in part (2) the same b must be minimal for 𝔪, since its µ-ordinarity is fed back into Corollary 6.1.4 at 𝔪, and must carry a lift of ρ_𝔪 in compactly supported cohomology, which is asserted without proof. The paper's own ingredients close the gap, so Theorem 6.3.1 is unaffected.

sourceIssues.locator: §6.3, proof of Theorem 6.3.1(1), p. 759 (not in arXiv v1)
sourceIssues.printed: It follows that there is some Π^S as in Lemma 5.5.1 whose Hecke eigenvalues lift 𝔪. Then Theorem 5.5.5 implies that there is a Galois representation r_{Π^S,ℓ}, whose reduction is the desired Galois representation ρ_𝔪.
sourceIssues.correction: It follows that there is some irreducible 𝔾(𝔸^S)-subrepresentation Π^S of BC^S([H_c(𝓘^b_Mant, ℚ̄_ℓ)]^{S ur}), as in Corollary 5.5.5 (cf. Corollary 5.5.2), whose Hecke eigenvalues lift 𝔪. Then Corollary 5.5.5 implies …
sourceIssues.reason: There is no Theorem 5.5.5: §5.5 consists of Lemma 5.5.1, Corollary 5.5.2, Remark 5.5.3, Theorem 5.5.4, Corollary 5.5.5, Remark 5.5.6, Theorem 5.5.7 and Lemma 5.5.8. The representation r_{Π^S,ℓ} with the Frobenius–Satake compatibility is produced by Corollary 5.5.5 (p. 745), whose hypothesis is exactly what the argument has just produced; Lemma 5.5.1 concerns Π^n⃗, not Π^S. arXiv v1 reads “some Π^n⃗ as in Lemma 5.5.1 … Then Theorem 5.5.3 implies”, which was correct there; in revision that theorem became Theorem 5.5.4 and Corollary 5.5.5, and the sentence was only partly updated.
